guidingQuestion: How does Earth's surface change through time, and how can we compare changes that are tiny or enormous, lightning-fast or unimaginably slow?
hook: A glacier can look frozen in place, yet every day it grinds, carries and drops rock, and that slow work, added up over many thousands of years, can reshape a whole valley.

objectives.text: Use uniformitarianism and evidence such as look-alike hoodoos around the world to explain how past landscapes formed and to predict how today's landscapes will change, while stating what the principle does not claim.

keyIdeas: Earth's surface is constantly reworked: weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces, erosion carries the pieces away, deposition drops them somewhere new, and uplift raises large areas of crust, usually very slowly.

Water, ice, wind, gravity, living things and chemical reactions all drive these changes. Most of them are Earth's other systems (air, water, ice and life) acting on rock, and gravity pulls on everything.

Changes happen at every spatial scale, from microscopic specks to the whole planet, and at every time scale, from a split second to billions of years. Our senses cover only the narrow human scale, so scientists use charts and models to compare the rest.

Size and speed don't automatically go together. A large asteroid impact can cool the entire planet within days, while a cave formation only tens of centimeters across takes thousands of years to grow. That is why scientists give both a time scale and a spatial scale.

Small, slow changes add up. Gust after gust of wind, each moving only a little sand, built the Namib Desert's towering dunes, and continents creeping a few centimeters a year can cross thousands of kilometers over Earth's history.

Sudden events such as landslides, flash floods, eruptions and asteroid impacts usually last from seconds to weeks (though some eruptions go on for years or far longer) yet can reshape land dramatically, and the conditions behind them often take a long time to build.

Uniformitarianism holds that the processes we can watch today also worked in the past and will keep working in the future. Matching hoodoos on several continents show the same processes acting alike in many places, which fits this idea, and modern geologists add that the rates of processes can change.

glossary.definition: The breakdown of rock at Earth's surface, either into smaller pieces by physical forces such as frost and grinding, or by chemical reactions that dissolve or change it. Weathering itself does not haul material away; that is erosion.
The picking up and carrying away of loosened rock material by moving water, wind, ice or gravity.
The settling and piling up of rock material in a new place after water, wind, ice or gravity has carried it there.
The rising of broad regions of Earth's crust, pushed by forces deep underground. It is usually very slow, and over millions of years it can raise whole mountain ranges.
The principle that the natural processes we can observe today also operated in the past and will continue in the future, so the present helps us read Earth's history.
The range of sizes or areas being considered, from microscopic to global, used to describe how much of Earth a process affects.
The range of durations being considered, from fractions of a second to billions of years, used to describe how long a process takes.
The sizes and times people can sense directly: lengths from about a millimeter to a few kilometers and times from seconds to years.
Weathering in which a chemical reaction changes or dissolves rock, as when weakly acidic water slowly dissolves limestone to open a cave.
A sudden, powerful event, such as an eruption, a landslide or an asteroid impact, that changes Earth's surface quickly and dramatically.
A hill or ridge of loose sand heaped up by the wind; some grow hundreds of meters tall.
Rock made of sand grains that were buried, packed tightly together and glued by mineral cement into solid stone.
A tall, thin pillar of rock, usually topped by a cap of tougher rock, left standing as weathering and erosion strip away the softer rock around it.

explorer.title: Break It, Move It, Drop It, Lift It
paragraphs: Solid rock looks permanent, but Earth's surface is always being reworked. Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces right where it sits. Erosion picks the pieces up and hauls them off. Deposition is what happens when the hauling slows down and the pieces settle and pile up in a new place.

Plenty of agents do this work. Water dissolves some rocks and washes loose grains along. Ice pries cracks apart, and glaciers scrape up rock and carry it off. Wind blows sand and dust. Gravity drags rock downhill. Living things grind and split rock too, even a beetle crunching across a dune. Most of these agents are Earth's other systems (air, water, ice and life) acting on rock; gravity is a force that pulls on all of them.

Some changes build land up instead of wearing it down. Uplift raises huge areas of crust, usually very slowly, pushed by forces deep underground, and over millions of years it can lift whole mountain ranges. Sand buried under more and more layers gets squeezed tight and glued by minerals into sandstone.

Limestone caves are a special kind of weathering. Rainwater picks up a little carbon dioxide and turns weakly acidic. Seeping through cracks for hundreds of thousands of years, it dissolves the limestone and opens up passages.

diagram.caption: One path rock material can take (one of many possible paths)
diagram.alt: A chain of five boxes joined by arrows. Solid rock, arrow labeled weathering, to loose grains. Loose grains, arrow labeled erosion by wind, water, ice or gravity, to grains on the move. Grains on the move, arrow labeled deposition, to layers of sand. Layers of sand, arrow labeled burial, packing and mineral cement, to sandstone. This is only one possible path; rock material can take many others.

edges.label: erosion by wind, water, ice or gravity

explorer.watchOut: Weathering and erosion are easy to mix up: weathering breaks rock, erosion moves it. Also, the textbook makes it sound as if the weight of overlying layers alone cements sand into sandstone. The weight packs the grains together, but minerals left behind by groundwater are what glue them into rock.

explorer.title: Two Rulers for Every Change
paragraphs: Scientists size up every Earth process with two rulers. One measures space: how much of Earth the process touches, from microscopic specks to the whole planet. The other measures time: how long the process takes, from a split second to billions of years.

Your senses work on the human scale, with lengths from millimeters to kilometers and times from seconds to years. Most of Earth's story happens far outside that window, so scientists use charts and models that stretch both rulers.

The two rulers don't move together. Dust from a large asteroid impact can cool the whole planet within days, while a cave formation only tens of centimeters across takes thousands of years to grow. Size alone doesn't tell you speed.

To fit everything on one page, the textbook's time-and-space chart leaps from microseconds to seconds to minutes to hours and on up to billions of years. That keeps quick and slow processes visible side by side, but it also means the chart is not drawn to an even scale.

diagram.caption: Some processes placed by space and by time (values from the lesson's chart and text)
diagram.alt: A table with three columns: example, space it affects, and time it takes. Rain splashing sand grains a few millimeters: human scale; seconds to minutes. A landslide moving rock and soil downhill: human scale, hundreds of meters; minutes. Dust from a large asteroid impact cooling Earth: global; days to years. Drips building a cave formation tens of centimeters wide: human scale; thousands of years. Ice sheets covering land in a glacial period: continental, millions of square kilometers; more than 10,000 years. A river carving the Grand Canyon: regional; about 5 million years. Uplift raising the Rocky Mountains: continental; tens of millions of years.

Landslide moves rock and soil downhill
Dust from a large asteroid impact cools Earth
Drips build a cave formation tens of cm wide

explorer.watchOut: Big does not mean slow, and small does not mean fast, so you always need both scales. Also, each step along the chart's time axis is a far bigger jump than the step before it, so distances on the chart don't show true proportions of time. Read each chart label carefully, too: the textbook's chart places pillow-sized stromatolite fossils at billions of years, but that number is how old the oldest ones are, not how long one took to form.

explorer.title: Slow Sums and Sudden Jolts
paragraphs: Most changes to Earth's surface are too slow to notice. Continents creep a few centimeters a year, and a single gust of wind moves only a thin skin of sand. But tiny changes repeated over thousands to millions of years add up: wind heaps grains into ripples and, on a much larger scale, into dunes, and many dunes together make a sand sea stretching hundreds of kilometers. The continents themselves have been shifting and changing for billions of years, and that long, slow history gave them their present shapes and positions.

Other changes arrive all at once. A landslide can rush down a slope in minutes, a flash flood can roar through a canyon in hours, and an eruption can bury land under lava within weeks. These events are brief, but they can remake a landscape.

Sudden events usually have slow backstories. Magma gathers underground for a long time before an eruption. Weathering weakens a slope before heavy rain or an earthquake sets it sliding. A hoodoo's pillar thins for thousands of years before its cap finally drops.
So slow and sudden are not rivals working separately. Slow change often sets the stage, and the sudden event is the moment the stage gives way.

diagram.caption: Sudden events and what came before them
diagram.alt: A table with three columns: sudden event, how long it lasts, and what came before. Landslide: minutes; weathering weakened the slope, then heavy rain or shaking set it off. Flash flood: hours; heavy rain fell in a short time, or water held back by a dam or ice jam was released. Volcanic eruption: often weeks, though some last years or far longer; magma collected beneath the surface over a long time. Hoodoo cap falling: seconds; weathering and erosion thinned the pillar for thousands of years. Large asteroid impact: moments, with cooling lasting days to years; the asteroid may have orbited the sun for billions of years.
rows: Weathering weakened the slope; heavy rain or shaking set it off
Heavy rain in a short time, or water held back by a dam or ice jam
Often weeks (some last years or far longer)
Magma collected beneath the surface over a long time
Weathering and erosion thinned the pillar for thousands of years
Moments; cooling lasts days to years
The asteroid may have orbited the sun for billions of years

explorer.watchOut: "Sudden" describes how fast an event happens, not that it came from nowhere. And a landform that looks the same after a year may still be changing, just too slowly for anyone to notice.

explorer.title: The Present Is the Key to the Past
paragraphs: Hoodoos, tall rock pillars wearing caps of tougher rock, stand in places as far apart as Alberta, Utah, Italy, Serbia and New Zealand. They are made of different rocks, yet they look alike because the same processes shaped them: weathering and erosion strip softer rock away faster than rock shielded by the cap.

Matching results in faraway places suggest that natural processes follow the same rules everywhere. Geologists take one more step: the processes working today also worked long ago and will keep working. This principle is called uniformitarianism, and it is often summed up as "the present is the key to the past."

That idea turns everyday observation into a time machine. Watch a river drop gravel where its current slows, and you can explain an old gravel layer far from any river. Watch a stone arch thin a little more each decade, and you can predict that someday it will fall.

Modern geologists add two cautions. The kinds of processes stay the same, but how fast they run can change with climate, rock type and other conditions. And sudden events, from landslides to asteroid impacts, are part of Earth's story too.

diagram.caption: Using today's processes to read the past and forecast the future
diagram.alt: A chain of four boxes joined by arrows. Watch a process happening today, arrow to find the traces that process leaves in rock and landforms, arrow to explain how an old feature formed, arrow to predict how today's landscape will change.

nodes.label: Find the traces it leaves in rock and landforms
Explain how an old feature formed
Predict how today's landscape will change

explorer.watchOut: Uniformitarianism does not mean Earth stays uniform or unchanging, and it does not mean every process always ran at the same speed. It means the same kinds of natural processes, following the same natural laws, are at work across time and place.

reviewFlags.issue: The Key Science Concept card 'Fossil Preservation' says stromatolites formed from the remains of algae colonies. Stromatolites are layered mounds built by microbial mats of cyanobacteria (once called blue-green algae) trapping sediment, not by true algae.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content mentions stromatolites only in the O2 explorer card's watch-out, as a chart-reading caution: the chart's billions-of-years placement is how old the oldest fossils are, not how long one took to form. Content never calls them algae. Reviser round 1 (2026-10-14) took them out of the O2 processes table, and the second review cycle moved the remaining mention from paragraph 3 (which defines time scale as how long a process takes) to the watch-out. No question tests what built them or their age.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept spread, 'Fossil Preservation' card (rendered)
evidence.supports: Pillow-sized fossils called stromatolites, said to come from algae colonies that lived 3.5 billion years ago, are placed at the human spatial scale and the billions-of-years time scale.

evidence.title: The Stromatolites of Glacier National Park
evidence.supports: Stromatolites are layered mounds of sediment built by cyanobacteria (once called blue-green algae), whose microbial mats trap sediment and grow over it.

reviewFlags.issue: The vocabulary box, Section 3 and the Lesson Summary say observable processes happened 'in the same way' in the past and act 'the same way everywhere'. Read literally, this suggests processes always ran at the same rate. Modern uniformitarianism keeps the same kinds of processes and natural laws, but rates and intensities can vary, and sudden events are part of Earth's history.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content defines uniformitarianism as the same processes acting through time and adds that rates can change (key idea 7; O4 explorer card and watch-out). L11-Q24 keys the 'same kind of process' claims and rejects 'each process ran at today's speed' and 'leave sudden events out of the past'. L11-Q23 repairs the 'uniform means unchanging' reading.

evidence.locator: Vocabulary box; Section 3. Patterns of Change
evidence.supports: Uniformitarianism is the idea that natural processes we can observe today happened in the same way in the past and will in the future; observing the present is the key to understanding the past.

evidence.title: Geologic Principles—Uniformitarianism
evidence.supports: Hutton argued that Earth's past must be explained by processes that can be seen happening now, and that slow processes acting over long spans can produce effects as great as sudden catastrophes; the idea is summed up as the present being the key to the past.

evidence.title: Uniformitarianism
evidence.supports: Modern geology keeps the idea that the same kinds of processes act through time but no longer requires uniform rates (gradualism); the speed and intensity of processes may vary, and there is good evidence for sudden, violent events as well as gradual change.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 gives continental motion as about 1-3 cm per year. Plates carrying continents move at different speeds; Australia, for example, moves about 7 cm per year (Geoscience Australia). The USGS spreading rates (under 2.5 to over 15 cm/yr) measure how fast two plates separate.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says continents move 'a few centimeters a year'. L11-Q16 uses a stated, steady 2.5 cm per year, and its conditions give the USGS range as seafloor-spreading rates, not the speed of one plate; it needs no change.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Slow and Fast Changes on Earth's Surface, Changes That Happen Slowly
evidence.supports: Continents are still moving, at about 1 to 3 cm per year.

evidence.title: Understanding plate motions (This Dynamic Earth)
evidence.supports: Seafloor-spreading rates (how fast two plates move apart at a ridge) differ from place to place: the Arctic Ridge spreads at less than 2.5 cm/yr, the East Pacific Rise at more than 15 cm/yr, and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge averages about 2.5 cm/yr.

evidence.title: Geocentric Datum of Australia 2020 (GDA2020)
evidence.supports: Because of plate motion, Australia has moved about 7 cm per year.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 says the weight of overlying material causes sand layers to become 'cemented together (to compact and eventually harden)'. This blends two steps. Weight compacts the grains, and cementation happens when minerals carried by groundwater are left between the grains and glue them.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content separates compaction from cementation. The glossary entry for sandstone, the O1 explorer card and its watch-out, and the L11-Q06 ordering item each name both steps.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Slow and Fast Changes on Earth's Surface, Changes That Happen Slowly
evidence.supports: The weight of overlying material is said to cement sand layers, compacting and hardening them into sandstone.

evidence.title: Sand Dunes to Sandstone
evidence.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, Zion National Park
evidence.supports: Buried dune sand was packed tighter by the weight of overlying sediment (compaction), and groundwater carrying dissolved calcium carbonate left mineral cement that glued the grains into the Navajo Sandstone.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 says caves form from 'a chemical reaction between the water and limestone'. That is true but incomplete: the water is weakly acidic (mostly carbonic acid from dissolved carbon dioxide), which is why it can dissolve limestone. The NPS adds that stream passages widen by about 1 mm per year at most.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says weakly acidic water dissolves limestone (glossary entry for chemical weathering, O1 explorer card). L11-Q05 keys that answer and its explanation uses the NPS 1 mm-per-year maximum.

evidence.locator: Section 2. Slow and Fast Changes on Earth's Surface, Changes That Happen Slowly
evidence.supports: A chemical reaction between water and limestone slowly dissolves the limestone, forming a cave over hundreds of thousands of years.

evidence.title: Solution Caves
evidence.supports: Solution caves form when weakly acidic water, usually carbonic acid from dissolved carbon dioxide, dissolves limestone along cracks and layers; stream passages grow at most about 1 mm per year, and many caves are hundreds of thousands to millions of years old.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 and its photo label say eruptions 'can last for several weeks'. Eruptions vary enormously: historic eruptions have lasted from under a day to thousands of years, and the median is about 7 weeks.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says eruptions often last weeks, though some last years or far longer (O3 explorer card and table; key idea 6). No question tests eruption length. L11-Q18 describes its eruption item explicitly as burying a valley within weeks, and L11-Q21 states the variation in its limitations.

evidence.supports: Some eruptions can last several weeks; the photo label also says several weeks.

evidence.title: How long do eruptions last?
evidence.supports: The median length of historic eruptions is about 7 weeks, but eruptions have lasted anywhere from less than a day to thousands of years.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 defines an asteroid as 'a large, mountain-sized chunk of rock'. Asteroids range from less than 10 m across to about 530 km (Vesta), so many are far smaller than mountains and a few are far larger.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content refers only to 'a large asteroid impact' and does not define asteroids by size. No question tests asteroid size.

evidence.supports: An asteroid is described as a large, mountain-sized chunk of rock orbiting the sun.

evidence.title: Asteroids: Facts
evidence.supports: Asteroids range in size from Vesta, about 530 km across, down to bodies less than 10 m across.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 2 says flash floods are caused by heavy rainfall over a short time. One sentence then says landslides and flash floods happen when heavy rain or earthquakes 'make unstable ground move', which fits landslides, not floods. NOAA's National Weather Service adds other causes of flash floods: a failed dam or levee, or the sudden release of water held back by an ice or debris jam.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content gives heavy rain in a short time as the usual cause and adds dam, levee and ice-jam releases. Earthquakes are linked only to landslides. L11-Q20 keys 'very heavy rain in a short time' and 'a dam or ice jam suddenly giving way'.

evidence.supports: Flash floods are caused by heavy rain over a very short time; landslides and flash floods are said to happen when heavy rain and earthquakes make unstable ground move.

evidence.title: Flood Safety Awareness Week - Flood Hazards
evidence.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service, Central Illinois Forecast Office
evidence.supports: Flash floods usually follow heavy rain within about 6 hours, and can also happen within hours or even minutes when a dam or levee fails or water held back by an ice or debris jam is suddenly released.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 1 places the Namib Desert in 'western Africa' (it lies along the southwest coast of Africa, mostly in Namibia) and gives its largest dunes as 240 m tall; NASA gives the tallest as about 325 m. The textbook's 80,000 km² of 'wind-blown sand' appears to describe the whole Namib Desert, which also includes rocky plains, not only wind-blown sand; NASA gives about 34,000 km² for the Namib Sand Sea. The 55-million-year figure is an estimate of the age of the desert itself (NASA, citing the United Nations Environment Programme), not a dated age of the sand.
reviewFlags.resolution: The textbook's Namib figures are treated as rough examples from the time it was written. No question tests the desert's area, its age or the exact dune height. L11-Q09 uses round, stated values (a 300 m dune, close to the height of the tallest Namib dunes, and a 2 mm grain), and its explanation gives both the textbook's 240 m and NASA's 325 m. Dated Namib dunes are thousands of years old (oldest sand about 5,700 years in a large linear dune; Bristow, Duller & Lancaster 2007), while NASA describes Dune 45's grains as about 5 million years old; L11-Q17 keys accumulation over thousands of years and more, not millions.

evidence.locator: Section 1, field-trip opening (p. 142); Many Small Changes Add Up to Large Changes, and Figure 1B (p. 143)
evidence.supports: The Namib Desert is placed in western Africa; some of its largest dunes are given as 240 m in height and 32 km in length, and the whole desert as more than 80,000 km² of windblown sand that built up over 55 million years.

evidence.title: Namib Sand Sea (Image of the Day, November 26, 2021)
evidence.supports: The Namib Sand Sea spans about 34,000 km² of coastal Namibia; its tallest dune, nicknamed Big Daddy, is about 325 m tall; Dune 45 is built of sands about 5 million years old; most of the sand comes from erosion to the south near the Orange River and is carried north along the coast.

evidence.title: Age and dynamics of linear dunes in the Namib Desert (Bristow, Duller & Lancaster, Geology 2007)
evidence.supports: Luminescence dating of a large Namib linear dune found its oldest sand about 5,700 years old, and the dune moved about 300 m sideways in 2,500 years, so big dunes are built and rebuilt over thousands of years.

evidence.title: Namibia's Protected Coast (Image of the Day, October 18, 2011)
evidence.supports: The Namib Desert is estimated to be 55 million years old and may be the oldest desert in the world, according to the United Nations Environment Programme; rocky plains lie north of the Kuiseb River, beyond the sand sea.

reviewFlags.issue: The lesson gives three different times for mountain-building uplift. The text says uplift 'can take place over the course of 100 million years'. The photo label reads 'hundreds of millions of years'. The Key Science Concept card says uplift built the Rocky Mountains 'over about 30 million years'.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content says uplift raises mountain ranges over millions to tens of millions of years. L11-Q10 asks only for relative order, using 'tens of millions of years' for the Rockies, and its neighbors in the order are minutes, hours, more than 10,000 years and billions of years, so the ranking does not depend on the exact figure.

evidence.locator: Section 2 text and photo label; Key Science Concept 'Mountain Formation' card (rendered)
evidence.supports: Uplift builds mountain ranges over very long spans: the text gives 100 million years, the photo label hundreds of millions of years, and the spread about 30 million years for the Rocky Mountains.

evidence.title: 2- Mountain Building (Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area)
evidence.supports: The Laramide uplift that raised this part of the Rocky Mountains started about 70 million years ago.

reviewFlags.issue: The Key Science Concept card 'Rock Formation' says eruptions add new material to Earth's surface 'up to hundreds of thousands of km² in days or months', and pairs this claim with a lava photo. Lava fields that large (for example, the Columbia River flood basalts, over 210,000 km²) took hundreds of flows over about a million years. Ash fall is different: ash from a large explosive eruption can blanket tens of thousands of km² within hours (Mount St. Helens in 1980 dropped ash over more than 57,000 km² in 9 hours), and the largest eruptions spread ash wider still. So the card's claim fails for lava but can fit ash fall.
reviewFlags.resolution: This claim is not used. Content says only that an eruption can bury land for many kilometers around within weeks, as Section 2 states.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept spread, volcanic 'Rock Formation' card (rendered; missing from OCR)
evidence.supports: Volcanic eruptions are said to add new material to Earth's surface, up to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, in days or months.

evidence.title: Columbia River Basalt Group Stretches from Oregon to Idaho
evidence.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Cascades Volcano Observatory
evidence.supports: Flood basalts covering more than 210,000 km² were built by more than 350 lava flows erupted from about 16.7 to 5.5 million years ago, with most of the volume erupted over about 1.1 million years.

evidence.title: How much ash was there from the May 18, 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens?
evidence.supports: About 540 million tons of ash fell over more than 57,000 km² (22,000 square miles) during the 9 hours of vigorous eruption on May 18, 1980.

reviewFlags.issue: The Key Science Concept card 'Crystal Formation' says crystals several meters across form when magma cools over tens of millions of years. The author could not verify this timing, and growth times for giant crystals vary widely.
reviewFlags.resolution: This claim is not used in any content or question.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept spread, 'Crystal Formation' card (rendered)
evidence.supports: Crystals several meters across are said to form as magma cools in Earth's interior over tens of millions of years.

reviewFlags.issue: Section 3 says hoodoos made of different rocks 'all formed the same way', and that weathering and erosion act the same way everywhere. The general recipe is shared (softer rock wears away faster than a resistant top). The details differ from place to place: at Bryce Canyon, for example, frost wedging and weakly acidic rain do most of the work, guided by layers with different amounts of mineral cement.
reviewFlags.resolution: Content describes hoodoos as shaped by the same general processes, with details that can vary. L11-Q25 keys 'the same processes shape rock alike in many places' and names the frost-wedging variation in its limitations. L11-Q26 keys the more resistant cap shielding the rock under it, which both the textbook and the NPS support.

evidence.supports: Hoodoos are rock pillars about 1.5 to 45 m tall, usually with a cap of more resistant rock that protects the rock under it; they form by weathering and erosion over thousands to millions of years, look unchanged from year to year, and can suddenly lose their caps when the pillar gets too thin.

evidence.locator: Section 3. Patterns of Change (uniformitarianism) and arch photo caption
evidence.supports: Similar hoodoos made of different rocks in different places show the same processes acting alike everywhere; the same processes act the same way across time; this principle is uniformitarianism, summed up as observing the present being the key to the past; the pictured arch is still eroding and will someday collapse.

evidence.title: Hoodoos
evidence.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, Bryce Canyon National Park
evidence.supports: Bryce Canyon's hoodoos are carved by frost wedging, as freezing water expands and pries rock apart, and by slightly acidic rain dissolving the calcium carbonate that binds the rock; layers with more of this cement resist weathering better than others.

All chart placements used in content (for example, landslide: human scale and minutes; asteroid cooling: global and days; glacial period: continental and thousands of years; Grand Canyon: regional and millions of years; stromatolites: human scale and billions of years) come from the renders.

evidence.locator: Key Science Concept: Earth Processes at Different Scales of Time and Space (rendered)
evidence.supports: The chart places processes on a space axis (atomic, microscopic, human, regional, continental, global, solar system, astronomical) and a time axis (microseconds to billions of years); the human scale runs from seconds to years and from millimeters to kilometers.

reviewFlags.issue: The vocabulary box and Section 2 present uplift only as a slow process (one that can take 100 million years). Mountain ranges do rise slowly overall, but large earthquakes can raise land suddenly: during the 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake the fault ruptured in about 4 minutes and land rose by as much as about 11 m on Montague Island.
reviewFlags.resolution: The glossary now says uplift is usually very slow and can raise mountain ranges over millions of years; key idea 1 and the O1 explorer card say 'usually very slowly'. Content never says uplift is always slow. L11-Q07, L11-Q10 and L11-Q18 test mountain-range uplift over millions of years, which stays slow, so they are unaffected.

evidence.locator: Vocabulary box; Section 2. Slow and Fast Changes on Earth's Surface, Changes That Happen Slowly
evidence.supports: Uplift is defined as forces deep underground raising large areas of crust, and it is listed among gradual processes that can take about 100 million years to build mountain ranges.

evidence.title: The 1964 Great Alaska Earthquake and Tsunami
evidence.publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, Alaska Science Center
evidence.supports: In the 1964 earthquake a 580-mile section of the fault ruptured in about 240 seconds, shaking lasted 4.5 minutes, some parts of the coast sank while others rose, and the maximum uplift, on Montague Island, was about 11 m (36 feet).
